steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for EvalCrafter, our benchmark for evaluating large text-to-video generation models. Motivate why current T2V evaluation is inadequate, describe how we build the prompts and evaluate along several aspects, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Large generative models: LLMs and text-to-image
- Progress in text-to-video generation, and the evaluation gap
- Our approach: prompt list, four evaluation aspects, alignment with user study
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Large generative models
  - ChatGPT and GPT4: human-level abilities in coding, math, even visual understanding; conversational interaction using any knowledge
  - visual content creation: Stable Diffusion (SD) and SDXL, most powerful publicly available T2I models, high-quality images from any text prompt
- T2V progress
  - early works Imagen-Viedo, Make-A-Video: cascaded models for direct video generation
  - LVDM, MagicVideo: use SD image priors, train temporal layers to generate videos efficiently
  - commercial services from text or images: Gen2, PikaLabs; technique details unavailable, not evaluated/compared with other methods
- Evaluation gap
  - current large T2V models only use GAN-based metrics like FVD
  - FVD = distribution matching between generated and real videos, not text prompt / video pairs
  - good evaluation should cover different aspects, e.g. motion quality, temporal consistency
  - like LLMs, some models not public, only generated videos accessible -> harder
  - evaluation progressed for LLM, MLLM, T2I but hard to use directly for video; motion and consistency ignored by previous works
- Our approach
  - very first step to evaluate general T2V models
  - prompt list: everyday objects, attributes, motions
  - balanced well-known concepts: start from meta types of real-world knowledge, extend with ChatGPT
  - also prompts from real-world users and T2I prompts
  - extract metadata (color, size, etc.) from prompts
  - four aspects: video quality, text-video alignment, motion quality, temporal consistency
  - objective metrics per aspect + user study for human scores
  - train regression coefficients per aspect to align with user preferences -> final model scores, evaluate new videos
- Contributions
  - first step evaluating large T2V; comprehensive prompt list with detailed annotations
  - aspects: visual quality, motion quality, temporal consistency, text-video alignment; human alignment, correlation analysis
  - conclusions and findings for future T2V development

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large generative models are attracting attention all over the world. For example, the well-known ChatGPT and GPT4 have shown human-level abilities in several aspects like coding, solving math problems, and even visual understanding, and they can be used to interact with people using any knowledge in a conversational way. For generative models for visual content creation, Stable Diffusion (SD) and SDXL are very important, since they are the most powerful publicly available models and can generate high-quality images from any text prompts.

Beyond text-to-image (T2I), using diffusion models for video generation has also progressed quickly. Early works (Imagen-Viedo, Make-A-Video) use cascaded models to generate videos directly. LVDM and MagicVideo were proposed to train temporal layers to generate videos efficiently, powered by the image generation priors in SD. Besides the academic papers, several commercial services can also generate videos from text or images, e.g., Gen2 and PikaLabs. We can not get the technique details of these services, and they are not evaluated and compared with other methods.

- Evaluation gap
  - current large T2V models only use GAN-based metrics like FVD: distribution matching with real videos, not text prompt / video pairs
  - should consider different aspects, e.g. motion quality, temporal consistency
  - some models not public, only generated videos -> harder
  - evaluation progressed for LLM, MLLM, T2I, but hard to apply to video; motion and consistency ignored
- Our approach
  - very first step for general T2V evaluation
  - prompt list (everyday objects, attributes, motions); meta types of real-world knowledge extended with ChatGPT; plus real-world user prompts and T2I prompts; metadata (color, size, etc.)
  - four aspects: video quality, text-video alignment, motion quality, temporal consistency
  - objective metrics + user study; regression coefficients per aspect aligned with user preferences
- Contributions
  - first step + prompt list with detailed annotations
  - four aspects, human alignment, correlation analysis
  - conclusions and findings for future T2V models

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large generative models are attracting attention all over the world. For example, the well-known ChatGPT and GPT4 have shown human-level abilities in several aspects like coding, solving math problems, and even visual understanding, and they can be used to interact with people using any knowledge in a conversational way. For generative models for visual content creation, Stable Diffusion (SD) and SDXL are very important, since they are the most powerful publicly available models and can generate high-quality images from any text prompts.

Beyond text-to-image (T2I), using diffusion models for video generation has also progressed quickly. Early works (Imagen-Viedo, Make-A-Video) use cascaded models to generate videos directly. LVDM and MagicVideo were proposed to train temporal layers to generate videos efficiently, powered by the image generation priors in SD. Besides the academic papers, several commercial services can also generate videos from text or images, e.g., Gen2 and PikaLabs. We can not get the technique details of these services, and they are not evaluated and compared with other methods.

But all current large text-to-video (T2V) models only use previous GAN-based metrics like FVD for evaluation. FVD only looks at the distribution matching between the generated video and the real videos, and not at the pairs between the text prompt and the generated video. We think a good evaluation method should consider metrics in different aspects, e.g., the motion quality and the temporal consistency. Also, like with large language models (LLMs), some models are not publicly available and we can only get access to the generated videos, which makes evaluation even harder. Evaluation has progressed quickly for large generative models, including LLM, MLLM, and T2I, but it is still hard to use these methods directly for video generation. The main problem is that, unlike T2I or dialogue evaluation, motion and consistency are very important for video generation, and previous works ignore them.

We make the very first step to evaluate general T2V models. First we build a comprehensive prompt list that contains various everyday objects, attributes, and motions. To get a balanced distribution of well-known concepts, we start from the well-defined meta types of real-world knowledge and use the knowledge of the LLM, i.e., ChatGPT, to extend our meta-prompt to a wide range. Besides the prompts generated by the model, we also select prompts from real-world users and T2I prompts. Then we obtain the metadata (e.g., color, size, etc.) from the prompt for further evaluation. Second, we assess the performance of large T2V models from four aspects, i.e., video quality, text-video alignment, motion quality, and temporal consistency. For each aspect we use several objective metrics as evaluation measures, and we do a user study to get human scores for these four aspects. Then we train coefficients of a regression model for each aspect, so the evaluation scores are aligned with user preferences. This lets us get the final model scores and evaluate new videos using the trained coefficients.

The contributions of our paper are:

- We make the first step of evaluating large T2V models and build a comprehensive prompt list with detailed annotations for T2V evaluation.

- We consider video visual quality, video motion quality, video temporal consistency, and text-video alignment for evaluating video generation. For each aspect we align with human opinions and verify the effectiveness of the proposed metric by correlation analysis.

- During the evaluation we also discuss several conclusions and findings, which might help further innovation and development of T2V models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The charm of large generative models is sweeping the world. For example, the well-known ChatGPT and GPT4 [1] have shown human-level abilities in several aspects, including coding, solving math problems, and even visual understanding, and can be used to interact with human beings using any knowledge in a conversational way. As for generative models for visual content creation, Stable Diffusion (SD) [2] and SDXL [3] play very important roles, since they are the most powerful publicly available models that can generate high-quality images from any text prompts.

Beyond text-to-image (T2I), taming diffusion models for video generation has also progressed rapidly. Early works (Imagen-Viedo [4], Make-A-Video [5]) utilize cascaded models for video generation directly. Powered by the image generation priors in SD, LVDM [6] and MagicVideo [7] have been proposed to train temporal layers to efficiently generate videos. Apart from academic papers, several commercial services can also generate videos from text or images, e.g., Gen2 [8] and PikaLabs [9]. Although we can not get the technique details of these services, they are not evaluated and compared with other methods. However, all current large text-to-video (T2V) models only use previous GAN-based metrics like FVD [10] for evaluation, which only concern the distribution matching between the generated video and real videos, rather than the pairs between the text prompt and the generated video. In contrast, we argue that a good evaluation method should consider metrics in different aspects, e.g., motion quality and temporal consistency. Also, similar to large language models (LLMs), some models are not publicly available and we can only access the generated videos, which further increases the difficulty of evaluation. Although evaluation has progressed rapidly for large generative models, including LLM [1], MLLM [11], and T2I [12], it is still hard to directly use these methods for video generation. The main problem is that, unlike T2I or dialogue evaluation, motion and consistency are very important to video generation, and previous works ignore them.

We make the very first step to evaluate general T2V models. In detail, we first build a comprehensive prompt list containing various everyday objects, attributes, and motions. To achieve a balanced distribution of well-known concepts, we start from the well-defined meta types of real-world knowledge and utilize the knowledge of the LLM, i.e., ChatGPT [1], to extend our meta-prompt to a wide range. Besides the prompts generated by the model, we also select prompts from real-world users and T2I prompts. After that, we obtain the metadata (e.g., color, size, etc.) from the prompt for further evaluation. Second, we assess the performance of large T2V models from four aspects, i.e., video quality, text-video alignment, motion quality, and temporal consistency. For each aspect, we employ several objective metrics as evaluation measures, and we conduct a user study to collect human scores for these four aspects. We then train coefficients of the regression model for each aspect, aligning evaluation scores with user preferences. This enables us to obtain the final model scores and evaluate new videos using the trained coefficients.

Overall, we summarize the contributions of our paper as:

- • We make the first step of evaluating large T2V models and build a comprehensive prompt list with detailed annotations for T2V evaluation.

- • We consider video visual quality, video motion quality, video temporal consistency, and text-video alignment for the evaluation of video generation. For each aspect, we align with human opinions and verify the effectiveness of the proposed metric by correlation analysis.

- • During the evaluation, we also discuss several conclusions and findings, which might contribute to further innovation and development of T2V models.

References:

[2] Robin Rombach, Andreas Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz, Patrick Esser, and Björn Ommer. High-resolution image synthesis with latent diffusion models, 2021.
